content.text: Matter exists in different states depending on how its particles are arranged and how they move. The three common states—solid, liquid, and gas—have very different properties, which can all be explained by the kinetic particle model.

The state of a substance depends on the balance between the kinetic energy of its particles (which tends to separate them) and the forces of attraction between them (which tend to hold them together).
(there's also plasma, but we'll focus on the three common states).
The nature of the particles themselves
Cannot move from place to place
Low kinetic energy compared to liquids and gases

| Property | Explanation |
|----------|------------|
| Fixed shape | Strong forces hold particles in place |
| Fixed volume | Particles closely packed, cannot compress |
| High density | Many particles per unit volume |
| Incompressible | No space between particles |
| Does not flow | Particles cannot move past each other |
Ice, iron, wood, diamond, salt, glass
Weaker bonds than solids, but still significant
Move in all directions, but stay close together

| Property | Explanation |
|----------|------------|
| No fixed shape | Particles can move past each other |
| Fixed volume | Particles still close together |

Move in straight lines between collisions

| Property | Explanation |
|----------|------------|
| No fixed shape | Particles move freely |

Air, oxygen, carbon dioxide, helium, steam

removes energy; particles slow down and bonds form
Temperature stays constant during a change of state (energy goes into breaking/forming bonds)
Explain why gases can be compressed but liquids cannot.
In gases, particles are far apart with large spaces between them. When pressure is applied, these spaces can be reduced, compressing the gas.
In liquids, particles are already close together with minimal space between them. There's no room for particles to move closer, so liquids cannot be compressed significantly.
Why does water change shape when poured from a bottle into a glass?

Liquid particles can move around each other. When water is poured, its particles flow and rearrange to take the shape of the new container (the glass). The particles are attracted to each other enough to stay together (fixed volume) but not strongly enough to maintain a fixed shape.
A fixed mass of gas is compressed to half its volume. How does this affect the particle behaviour?
Particles are now twice as close together
Same number of particles in smaller volume
More frequent collisions with container walls
Pressure increases (approximately doubles if temperature is constant)
Hydraulic systems (brakes, lifts) work because liquids are incompressible—pressure applied to a liquid is transmitted equally throughout.
Pneumatic systems use compressed gases. The compressibility of gases allows energy to be stored and cushioning effects.
Gases expand when heated and become less dense, causing them to rise. This drives convection currents and weather patterns.
Pressure cookers increase pressure, raising the boiling point of water. Food cooks faster at the higher temperature.

During a change of state, the temperature stays constant even though energy is being supplied. Students often incorrectly state that the temperature rises throughout heating. The energy goes into breaking or forming bonds, not increasing kinetic energy.

Solids have a fixed shape and fixed volume. Liquids have no fixed shape but a fixed volume. Gases have no fixed shape and no fixed volume. These properties arise directly from how particles are arranged and how strongly they attract each other.
— The visible "steam" from a kettle is actually tiny water droplets (condensed liquid). True steam (water vapour) is invisible.
— Most common gases are colourless, but some gases have colour (e.g., chlorine is green-yellow, bromine vapour is brown).
— Solid particles vibrate constantly; they just don't move from their positions.
— During the change of state, temperature remains constant while energy breaks bonds.
"Ice is less dense because particles are further apart"
— Actually, ice has a special crystal structure with spaces, making it less dense despite being solid.

Matter exists in three common states: solid, liquid, gas
Fixed shape and volume, particles vibrate in fixed positions
Fixed volume, no fixed shape, particles move around each other
No fixed shape or volume, particles move randomly at high speed
Density: solid ≈ liquid >> gas (with some exceptions like ice)
Compressibility: only gases are easily compressed (spaces between particles)
State changes involve energy transfer without temperature change
The kinetic particle model explains all macroscopic properties

| Property | Solid | Liquid | Gas | |----------|-------|--------|-----| | Shape | Fixed | Takes container shape | Fills container | | Volume | Fixed | Fixed | Variable | | Compressibility | Incompressible | Almost incompressible | Easily compressed | (explanation with physics reasoning)
Perfume molecules diffuse through the air.
They move randomly at high speed, colliding with air molecules, gradually spreading from high concentration near the source to low concentration across the room. (explanation with physics reasoning)
In a solid, particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces of attraction.
They can only vibrate about these positions, so the solid maintains a rigid, fixed shape. (explanation with physics reasoning)
Gas particles move randomly at high speeds and collide with the container walls.
Each collision exerts a small force; the combined effect of billions of collisions per second produces a measurable pressure on the walls. (explanation with physics reasoning)
— 20°C is below the melting point of 40°C. (explanation with physics reasoning)
— 100°C is above the melting point (40°C) but below the boiling point (150°C). (explanation with physics reasoning)
— 200°C is above the boiling point of 150°C. (explanation with physics reasoning)
Ice has a crystalline structure with open spaces between molecules

, making it less dense than liquid water (920 kg/m³ vs 1000 kg/m³). Because ice is less dense, it floats on the surface. This is vital for aquatic life because the floating ice layer insulates the water below, preventing lakes and rivers from freezing solid and allowing organisms to survive in the liquid water beneath. (explanation with physics reasoning)
Very high density (~7900 kg/m³). Particles are closely packed in a regular crystalline arrangement with strong metallic bonds. (comparison)
High density (~13,600 kg/m³). Particles are close together but irregularly arranged, able to slide past each other. (comparison)
Very low density (~1.3 kg/m³). Particles are far apart with large spaces between them, moving randomly at high speed. (comparison)
